These concerns can be mitigated by safeguards like price caps or bill protection programs, and by customer education that emphasizes the opportunity that dynamic pricing creates to access low-cost electricity. If customer participation in dynamic prices were completely random, the flexibility potential could be thought to scale linearly with the fraction of customers that adopt load flexibility technologies. However, if customers with more flexibility potential were assumed to be the “first adopters” of such tariffs, we can start to uncover the significant impacts that a small portion of customers can make. Figure 38 shows the cumulative flexibility potential across the customer base for each end use (in each sector) modeled in this study. The left panel of Figure 38 shows the potential as a fraction of the total for that specific end use, while the right panel shows the absolute 57 magnitude of the potential, such that it can be compared across end uses. Hypothetically, if we assume that only 10% of customers will participate in dynamic pricing, and that they are the 10% with the largest potential, we find that 20% of the potential for most end uses will be captured. For commercial cooling and heating, the top 10% of customers account for 30% and 40% of the end use potential, respectively, while for crop irrigation customers you only need 10% participation to realize more than half of the flexibility potential. Further, we can see (in the right panel of Figure 38) that the top 10% of commercial cooling customers generate as much flexibility potential as the top 10% of residential cooling customers. This is significant because there is an order of magnitude fewer commercial customers than residential customers, and non-residential customers who are already used to managing their electricity consumption in sophisticated ways may be more amenable to adopting dynamic prices. While the total flexibility of crop irrigation is approximately the same as that 10% of residential and commercial cooling, only 25% of those sites are needed to obtain 80% of that potential, and there is a further order of magnitude fewer row crop sites as there are commercial cooling customers in the state. Note that the above discussion pertains to the technical potential results as quantified by the avoided cost metric. When also considering the need to achieve a certain payback period, the potential of certain end uses (namely commercial cooling) will be impacted by the dynamic price design scenario, as discussed in Section 3.4.4. Therefore, assumptions around tariff selection and the differences in likely uptake of dynamic pricing across different customer groups may interact with the differences across tariff design scenarios in interesting ways. More directly, the potential lost in the commercial cooling end use by moving to a Mild design scenario (when considering short payback period potential) may have an outsized impact if it is expected that commercial customers will be more amenable to dynamic pricing and enroll in larger numbers than customers in other sectors. 58 Figure 38.
